lesson.title: Taming Very Big and Very Small Numbers: Scientific Notation
lesson.summary: Scientific notation writes any number as a coefficient between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, giving chemists a compact and unambiguous way to handle the extreme scales that show up from atoms to moles.
lesson.body:
Chemistry constantly deals with numbers that are absurdly large or absurdly small for ordinary decimal notation to handle comfortably. A single mole of any substance contains 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 particles, and a single water molecule has a mass of about 0.0000000000000000000000299 grams. Writing numbers like these out in full is not just tedious, it is also a serious source of counting errors, since a misplaced zero among twenty others is easy to miss. Scientific notation solves this problem by expressing any number as a coefficient between 1 and 10, multiplied by 10 raised to some whole number exponent.

To convert a large number into scientific notation, move the decimal point to the left until only one nonzero digit remains before it, and count how many places you moved it. That count becomes the positive exponent on 10. Avogadro's number, 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000, becomes 6.02 x 10^23 because the decimal point moved 23 places to the left. To convert a small number, move the decimal point to the right until one nonzero digit sits before it, and that count becomes a negative exponent. The mass of a water molecule, 0.0000000000000000000000299 g, becomes 2.99 x 10^-23 g because the decimal point moved 23 places to the right. In both directions, moving the decimal point to the left corresponds to a positive exponent, because you are effectively dividing by powers of ten and must multiply by an equal power to compensate, while moving it to the right corresponds to a negative exponent for the reverse reason.

Scientific notation also makes it far easier to keep track of significant figures, which is exactly why it connects so closely to that earlier concept. The coefficient in scientific notation shows only the digits that were actually measured or are otherwise significant, with no ambiguity about whether trailing zeros count. Writing a mass as 3.0 x 10^2 g unambiguously communicates two significant figures, while writing the same value as 300 g leaves a reader guessing whether the zeros are meaningful or just placeholders.

Multiplying and dividing numbers in scientific notation follows the normal rules of exponents: multiply or divide the coefficients directly, and add or subtract the exponents. For example, multiplying the mass of one water molecule, 2.99 x 10^-23 g, by Avogadro's number, 6.02 x 10^23, models finding the molar mass of water: (2.99 x 6.02) x 10^(-23 + 23) = 18.0 x 10^0 = 18.0 g/mol, a value that matches water's known molar mass closely, since water is built from two hydrogen atoms near 1.01 g/mol each and one oxygen atom near 16.00 g/mol, summing to about 18.02 g/mol.

Adding or subtracting numbers in scientific notation requires an extra step: the exponents must first be made equal before the coefficients can be combined. Adding 3.2 x 10^4 and 5.0 x 10^3 requires rewriting 5.0 x 10^3 as 0.50 x 10^4 so both terms share the same power of ten, then adding the coefficients: 3.2 + 0.50 = 3.7, giving a final answer of 3.7 x 10^4. Skipping this step and adding the coefficients directly without matching exponents is one of the most common errors students make, and it is worth checking every time before combining terms.
